newsitem.title: CHINA: China 1996 grain output seen vastly under-reported.
newsitem.headline: China 1996 grain output seen vastly under-reported.

text.p: China's total grain output in 1996 has been understated by more than 10 million tonnes, an agriculture expert said on Thursday.
China's total grain crop in 1996 was 502 million tonnes, compared with the official figure of 490 million, said X. Lyn Wu, general manager of East-West Consultants Ltd.
"The grain crop in 1996 was larger than people generally realise and larger than the government wants people to believe," Wu said.
"They (Chinese officials) are trying to understate the real crop because they want the farmers to keep planting," Wu said in an interview.
Officials fear farmers would not plant grain if they thought stocks were high and prices would be low, he said.
He predicted the 1997 total crop at 504 million tonnes.
Corn exports, more than two million tonnes so far for 1997, would continue in order to ease silos before the summer wheat harvest due to begin soon, he said.

"If the political clouds clear, we will see more corn exports. Now we are saying three million tonnes (for 1997)," he said, adding that he believed 2.4 million tonnes had been exported between January and May 1997.
Around 10 percent of the corn crop, which he put at 126.2 million tonnes in 1996, would be wasted. Corn waste in a normal year was between five and eight percent, he said.
China resumed corn exports in January 1997, after banning overseas sales in December 1994 amid shortages. Corn exports have been politically sensitive ever since due to inflation.
A good crop last year has led to bulging storage facilities in the northern growing areas. State media has said six million tonnes have already been shipped to the south.
China's government has yet to release a detailed breakdown of the 1996 crop. Traders and diplomats have said corn accounted for 127 million tonnes, rice 191 million and wheat 109 million.
Wu said 1996 wheat output was 111.9 million, and rice 198.4 million tonnes.
Wheat production in 1997 would rise to 116 million tonnes, he said, keeping imports in the year to end-August 1997 to 4.8 million tonnes.
Wheat consumption in China had also been underestimated, he said, but refused to elaborate before a detailed East-West report due in a couple of months.
Traders and industry sources put annual wheat consumption at 115 million tonnes, rising at one to 1.5 percent a year.
Wu said consumption growth could actually fall over time and within 15 years China might not need to import any wheat.
"If this push for more wheat production goes on, then China will not even need to import high quality wheat," he said.
"Quality is not a major consideration now, quantity is the major factor," he said. Even in high production years, China needs to import high quality wheat for flour millers.
"Imports will continue for now, but give it 15 years and we will not see any wheat imports in the substantial sense," he said. "Below one million tonnes (a year) it becomes insignificant."

His figures were based on thorough research at grassroots levels, he said, adding that analysts from East-West, which is affiliated with U.S. crop and weather forecaster Sparks, scoured China for their information.
